newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-All but Greece, Italy meet EMU deficit test.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-All but Greece, Italy meet EMU deficit test.

text.p: The European Commission painted a rosy view of the prospects for the European Union's single currency on Wednesday, saying only Italy and Greece were currently missing the deficit target needed to qualify.

Germany and France, the two economic powerhouses essential to economic and monetary union (EMU), were both seen squeezing in with deficits this year forecast at 3.0 percent of gross domestic product -- exactly the target set by the Maastricht Treaty.
Spain and Portugal also were seen just making the cut, with 3.0 percent.

"(It is my conviction) that a majority of member states will meet the requirements for pariticpation in the euro," EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said following release of the forecasts.
The news for Italy, one of the countries keenest to be in the first wave to move to the euro, was mixed.
The Commission said it was running a deficit to GDP ratio of 3.2 percent this year, missing the target. But it offered soothing words to go along with the report.
"This (3.2 percent) may become 3.0 percent of GDP if the (budgetary) measures already taken have full effectiveness and, if necessary, additional measures are introduced," it said.
But the forecasts also implied that Italy's finances were far from stable over the long term, noting that Rome was expected to run a deficit of 3.9 percent of GDP in 1998.

Release of the Commission figures -- which EU sources and financial analysts say are drafted under tremendous political pressure -- was delayed for close to an hour because of a longer-than-expected debate among members of the Commission.

On the financial markets, which had already discounted much of the news, the lira slipped on news of the 3.2 percent figure but advanced again on the Commission's suggestion that Italy could still make the target this year.
Some financial analysts have dismissed the Commission's twice-year forecasts as too political.
"This is another set of forecasts thrown into the pot and the EU is going to be viewed as biased," Roger Francis, senior analyst of IBJ International, said before the figures were released.
Germany's six leading economic research institutes forecast on Tuesday that Bonn's deficit to GDP ratio this year would be 3.2 percent.
A Portuguese newspaper also quoted the International Monetary Fund's latest outlook as predicting Germany would hit a 3.3 percent mark this year.
In a broad comment, the Commission said the EU's economies were recovering and output would continue to grow this year and next, helped by the strength of the dollar.
De Silguy said the only dark cloud on the horizon was the bloc's unemployment rate, forecast at 10.6 percent of the total workforce this year.
